1755-lisbon-earthquake: The earthquake struck at about 09:40 local time on Saturday, 1 November 1755, the Christian feast of All Saints. Seismologists estimate its magnitude at 7.7 or greater, with an epicentre in the Atlantic about 200 km west-southwest of Cape St. Vincent. Contemporary reports give a duration of three and a half to six minutes and describe fissures 5 metres wide in the city centre. Survivors fled to the docks and watched the sea recede; about 40 minutes later a tsunami engulfed the harbour and downtown area, followed by two more waves. Candles lit for the feast were knocked over, and the fires grew into a firestorm that burned for hours.

Damage was widespread beyond Lisbon. Most coastal towns of the Algarve were heavily damaged, except Faro, which was sheltered by the sandy banks of the Ria Formosa. Funchal on Madeira and the ports of the Azores suffered, and the tsunami struck Cadiz and the coast of North Africa. Waves reached Martinique and Barbados, and a three-metre wave hit Cornwall. Economic historian Álvaro Pereira estimated that of Lisbon's population of about 200,000, between 30,000 and 40,000 died, with perhaps another 10,000 in Morocco.

About 85 per cent of Lisbon's buildings were destroyed, among them the Royal Ribeira Palace, whose 70,000-volume library, paintings and royal archives were lost, along with records of the voyages of Vasco da Gama and other early navigators. King Joseph I and the court had left the city after Mass and survived. The prime minister, Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, 1st Marquis of Pombal, is reported to have answered the question of what to do with the words "Bury the dead and heal the living". Many corpses were buried at sea against the wishes of the Church, the army was deployed, and more than thirty people were publicly executed as looters.

On 4 December 1755 the chief engineer Manuel da Maia presented four plans, from abandoning Lisbon to building a new city. The king and Pombal chose the last, razing the Baixa quarter and laying out rectilinear streets; the Pombaline buildings are among the earliest seismically protected constructions in Europe. Pombal also sent a questionnaire on the shock, the sea and the fires to every parish, and the priests' answers, still kept in the Torre do Tombo, have led him to be seen as a forerunner of modern seismology. Voltaire drew on the disaster in Candide and a poem, attacking the idea that this is the best of all possible worlds, and Immanuel Kant published three texts on it in 1756.
1936-summer-olympics: Berlin won the right to host the 1936 Games over Barcelona at the 29th IOC Session in 1931, when the host was decided for the first time by a vote of each IOC member. The result was 43 votes for Berlin and 16 for Barcelona, whose prospects were probably weakened by the uncertainty that followed the proclamation of the Second Spanish Republic days before the Session. The Games were awarded under the Weimar Republic, but after the Nazi takeover of January 1933 the regime saw them as international propaganda.

To project an image of a peaceful, tolerant Germany, the authorities took down signs reading Jews not welcome for the duration. In July 1936 Berlin's police were authorised to detain the city's Romani and confine them in a camp at Marzahn. The German Olympic Committee effectively barred Jewish and Roma athletes. The high jumper Gretel Bergmann was dropped after equalling the German record, and the fencer Helene Mayer, who had one Jewish parent, was the only athlete of Jewish descent on the German team. Campaigns to boycott or relocate the Games arose in several countries but failed, and forty-nine nations competed, then the largest number.

The opening ceremony took place on 1 August 1936, with the airship Hindenburg flying over the Olympic Stadium, which seated about 100,000. These were the first Games to be televised, with over 70 hours of coverage to public viewing rooms, and the first with a torch relay carrying a flame from Olympia to the host city, organised by Carl Diem. Jesse Owens of the United States won four gold medals in the sprints and the long jump.

Germany topped the medal table with 101 medals, 38 of them gold, which includes 12 medals in art competitions, and the United States was second with 57. Leni Riefenstahl recorded the Games in her two-part film Olympia, released in 1938.

Historians widely regard the Games as a major propaganda success for the Nazi regime, though they differ on how far it reached. David Clay Large argues that the effect on Germany's international standing was limited, while at home the Games helped the still-insecure Hitler consolidate his power. The story that Hitler snubbed Owens is not supported by the evidence. No Olympic Games were held for the next 12 years because of the Second World War.
1954-guatemalan-coup-detat: The Guatemalan Revolution began in 1944, when a popular uprising led by students and middle-class citizens toppled the military ruler Jorge Ubico. Juan José Arévalo, elected president, introduced a minimum wage, a liberal labor code and wider suffrage. His successor Jacobo Árbenz, elected in 1950, drafted an agrarian reform bill that transferred uncultivated land from large landowners to poor laborers. Árbenz also legalized the communist Guatemalan Party of Labour, though he chose a moderate capitalist approach. The United States government, in the Cold War, was predisposed to see the revolution as communist.

The United Fruit Company, the largest landowner in Guatemala, had 550,000 acres of which only 15 percent was cultivated, so most of it came under the agrarian law of 1952. It lobbied the United States to act. President Harry S. Truman authorized Operation PBFortune in 1952, which was aborted quickly. His successor Dwight D. Eisenhower, who had promised to roll back communism, authorized the CIA to carry out Operation PBSuccess in August 1953.

The operation had a budget of 2.7 million dollars for psychological warfare and political action, and the CIA armed and trained a force of 480 men led by Carlos Castillo Armas. Its plans included lists of people to be assassinated. Before the invasion, propaganda reached Latin America and a campaign of threats was directed at likely loyalists of Árbenz. Castillo Armas crossed the border on 18 June 1954, while aircraft bombed Guatemala City and Chiquimula.

The invasion force did poorly in the field, and most of its offensives were defeated. But the bombing and fear of a United States invasion unsettled the Guatemalan army. Árbenz at first meant to arm civilians but gave arms only to the army. By 25 June officers at Zacapa were reporting that the army would not fight, and they asked him to resign. He did so on 27 June. A military junta followed, and Castillo Armas became president ten days later after negotiations in San Salvador.

Castillo Armas banned opposition parties, imprisoned and tortured opponents and reversed the revolution's social reforms. In the first months his government executed many supporters of Árbenz, with estimates from hundreds to five thousand. He was assassinated by a member of his guard in 1957. The coup was widely criticised abroad and strengthened anti-American sentiment in Latin America. The CIA's Operation PBHistory sought evidence of Soviet influence among Árbenz-era documents and found none. A civil war began in 1960 and lasted until 1996. In 1999 President Bill Clinton apologised for United States support of military regimes, and in 2011 President Álvaro Colom publicly apologised to Árbenz's family.
1988-armenian-earthquake: The region lies on an active seismic belt that stretches from the Alps to the Himalayas, produced by the convergence of the Arabian and Eurasian plates. The earthquake occurred along a known thrust fault 60 kilometres long, parallel to the Caucasus range, about 40 kilometres south of the mountains. In the months before, large demonstrations had been held in Yerevan, from February 1988, for democracy and for the unification of Nagorno-Karabakh with Armenia, and a state of emergency was declared in November.

The earthquake struck on 7 December 1988 at 11:41 local time, with a surface-wave magnitude of 6.8 and a maximum intensity of X on the MSK scale. The rupture began at a depth of 5 kilometres on the Alavar thrust fault, and five sub-events occurred in the first eleven seconds; an aftershock of local magnitude 5.8 followed four minutes and twenty seconds later. Between 25,000 and 50,000 people were killed and up to 130,000 injured. Spitak, Leninakan (Gyumri) and Kirovakan (Vanadzor) were greatly affected, as were smaller villages.

Many buildings collapsed, often without survival space, and most hospitals fell, killing two-thirds of their doctors and destroying equipment and medicine. A US team of engineers found that building inadequacies were the primary reason the strong but not huge earthquake was so destructive, with freezing temperatures adding to the toll. Leninakan suffered more than Kirovakan at a similar distance, possibly because of a sedimentary layer 300–400 metres thick beneath it. Rescue work ended in late December.

Mikhail Gorbachev, who was in New York, returned at once, and the Kremlin formally asked the United States for help, a sign of easing Cold War tensions. A hundred and thirteen countries sent aid, and the relief effort was the largest foreign cooperation in the Soviet Union since the Second World War.

A Soviet Ilyushin Il-76 crashed at Leninakan with nine crew and 69 military personnel, and a Yugoslav Antonov An-12 crashed at Yerevan the next day, killing seven. Gorbachev set aside 5 billion rubles for recovery. The French singer Charles Aznavour and Georges Garvarentz recorded the song Pour toi Arménie, whose sales funded 47 schools and three orphanages. In 1989 officials planned new building codes and decided that Leninakan would be moved several kilometres to the southwest.
1989-tiananmen-square-protests-and-massa: After Mao Zedong's death in 1976 and the arrest of the Gang of Four, Deng Xiaoping launched a program of economic reform called reform and opening up. He promoted allies to top posts: Zhao Ziyang became Premier in 1980 and Hu Yaobang became General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party in 1982. The reforms dismantled Mao-era guarantees such as lifetime employment in state-owned enterprises, the so-called iron rice bowl, which contributed to worker unrest over layoffs and inflation. Common grievances by 1989 included inflation, corruption, the limited preparedness of graduates for the new economy and restrictions on political participation.

The protests began after the sudden death of Hu Yaobang from a heart attack on 15 April 1989, which many students linked to his forced resignation. Mourners gathered around the Monument to the People's Heroes in Tiananmen Square, and within days the posters on campuses spoke of corruption, democracy and freedom of the press. Student protesters called for greater political accountability, constitutional due process and freedom of speech, while workers' protests centred on inflation and the economic reforms. At the height, on 17 May, about one million people were assembled in the square. A student-led hunger strike in May spread the protests to some 400 cities.

The leadership was divided. Zhao Ziyang favoured dialogue and a soft approach, while Premier Li Peng argued that stability overrode all else; they clashed at a meeting on 1 May. The State Council declared martial law on 20 May and mobilised at least 30 divisions, but crowds in the suburbs blocked the army, and it withdrew on 24 May. A meeting of the party leadership on 1 June decided to clear the square. Troops advanced into central Beijing on the early morning of 4 June and clashed with demonstrators trying to block them, and most of the killings took place along Chang'an Avenue in the western suburbs.

The death toll is disputed. An official announcement soon afterwards put it at about 300, and the Beijing Party Secretary Li Ximing reported a confirmed toll of 241 on 19 June. Other estimates range from several hundred to the low thousands, with thousands more wounded. On 13 June the Beijing Public Security Bureau ordered the arrest of 21 student leaders.

Western governments imposed arms embargoes, and the government purged officials thought sympathetic to the protests and built up its riot-control forces. Political reforms begun in 1986 halted, and market-oriented economic reforms were later accelerated after Deng Xiaoping's southern tour in 1992. The Chinese government calls the events the political turmoil between the spring and summer of 1989, and in China they are known as the June Fourth Incident.
1992-summer-olympics: On 17 October 1986 Barcelona was chosen to host the Games at the 91st IOC Session in Lausanne, Switzerland. It won over Amsterdam, Belgrade, Birmingham, Brisbane and Paris, with a majority of 47 votes from 85 of the 89 IOC members voting by secret ballot. Barcelona was the second-largest city in Spain and the capital of Catalonia, and the hometown of the then IOC president Juan Antonio Samaranch, who abstained. New Delhi had announced a bid but withdrew in March 1986. Beginning in 1994 the IOC decided to hold the Summer and Winter Games in alternating even-numbered years, so 1992 was the last year both were staged together.

At the opening ceremony the cauldron was lit by the Paralympic archer Antonio Rebollo, who shot a flaming arrow over its top to ignite the gas rising from it, a method designed so that a miss could not land the arrow in the stadium. A recording of the song Barcelona, by Freddie Mercury and Mike Moran, played at the start; Mercury had died eight months earlier. Amigos Para Siempre, by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Don Black, was sung at the closing ceremony by Sarah Brightman and José Carreras. The official mascot was Cobi, a Catalan sheepdog in cubist style designed by Javier Mariscal.

The programme had 257 events in 25 sports, with Basque pelota, roller hockey and taekwondo as demonstration sports. A total of 169 nations sent 9,356 athletes. Twelve of the former Soviet republics formed a Unified Team, which topped the medal table with 45 gold and 112 medals in all. Estonia and Latvia sent their own teams for the first time since 1936, and Lithuania for the first time since 1928. Germany competed as one team after reunification in 1990, and South Africa returned after a 32-year ban over apartheid. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was barred by UN sanctions, though individual athletes took part as Independent Olympic Participants.

The Games were the first since the end of the Cold War and the first unaffected by boycotts since 1972. In the women's 10,000 metres, the Ethiopian winner Derartu Tulu and the South African Elana Meyer ran a victory lap hand in hand. Before the Games, between 29 June and 14 July 1992, Spanish police arrested 45 Catalan pro-independence activists, journalists and politicians in Operation Garzón; political activists argue it was used to weaken the left-wing independence movement. ETA offered a truce on 10 July, which the Spanish government rejected, and no attack came during the Games.
The Games changed Barcelona. The Olympic Village and Olympic Port at Poblenou opened the city to the sea, ring roads were built, and El Prat airport gained two new terminals.
